title: Fig and Comet's Hollow Mystery
markdown:
A bedside lamp, still warm from the day, was the only glow in the room. Outside, the moon was a sliver of pearl. Leo slept, dreaming of faraway lands. For Fig the rat and Comet the squirrel, the house had gone quiet enough to try the window.

“Are you really sure, Comet?” Fig whispered. Whiskers twitched. The glass felt like a thin wall between the safe indoors and the wild night. His heart, usually a steady seed-crunching rhythm, fluttered.

Comet was already halfway out, copper fur catching moonlight. “Sure as a nut is nutty. The Big Oak whispered it when the wind sighed. Old Man Willow heard it from the stream. Tonight the Whispering Hollow finally whispers its deepest secret.”

The Whispering Hollow lay just beyond the ancient churchyard gate: gnarled trees, a silence that sometimes felt watchful. Grown-ups told children to avoid it. Fig believed in facts and sunflower seeds. Comet believed in anything faster than sitting still.

They slipped across the dewy lawn. Grass tickled Fig’s paws. The air smelled of damp earth, crushed leaves, and the faintest night-blooming jasmine. The churchyard gate creaked like an elderly gentleman clearing his throat.

The path wound through leaning gravestones painted silver and deep grey. Beyond the last weathered stone stood the signpost, wood worn smooth, once-painted words faded to blurriness. Around it a cloud of fireflies bloomed, pulsing like scattered stars, so the post seemed to float in a constellation of its own. Fig and Comet stopped there without meaning to. The lights did not hurry. They simply gathered, warmed the old wood, and made the faded letters look almost readable again. Jasmine and damp moss mixed in the still air. For a few breaths the hollow was only a dark line of trees, and the mystery was only this: that a worn post could look like a floating lantern if enough small things agreed to glow.

Comet breathed a rare sort of wonder. “The entrance.” He scampered up a low stone wall and peered toward the dark line of trees.

They crept closer. Ancient branches twisted like arthritic fingers. The silence was not empty; it was waiting. Then a flurry of chirps erupted from a hawthorn bush, scattering moths.

“Oh, it’s terrible,” trilled a robin, red breast puffing. “Poor Mrs Higgins, her prize-winning petunia. Completely ruined. Torn to shreds.”

“And the acorns. Not a single one left on the ground. Blown away, they say. Into the hollow, no doubt. Such a wicked wind.”

Fig blinked. “Petunias? Acorns? I didn’t see any ruined petunias on the path.”

Comet’s bounce deflated a little. “I thought we were investigating whispers, not garden disasters.”

The robins swooped to a low branch, beady eyes on the pair. “You two must do something. The hollow is a menace tonight. It swallowed all the best acorns and flattened Mrs Higgins’ prize petunia with its breath.”

Fig’s logical mind raced. “How could a hollow swallow acorns? Acorns don’t have mouths. And petunias don’t usually get flattened by breath.” He nudged Comet. “Did you see any flattened petunias on the way here?”

Comet’s tail flicked. “Not a petal out of place. And I saw loads of acorns near the old oak. Perfectly intact.”

The hollow was innocent. The terrible deeds were wind, a bit of clumsy foraging, and robin gossip that had got out of hand. Other creatures, drawn by the alarm, were starting to look nervous: a cautious rabbit behind ferns, a badger with a twitching nose. They all peered toward the shadowy entrance.

“This is most inefficient,” Fig muttered. “A waste of perfectly good nocturnal energy.”

“We have to tell them,” Comet declared, scampering onto a sapling, ready to broadcast.

“Patience,” Fig said. He understood how a whisper could grow into a roar if left unchecked. “We just need to remind everyone of what is real.”

With a burst of courage that did not match his stout frame, Fig hopped onto a smooth grey stone. Damp earth in his lungs. “Excuse me.” Small, clear, cutting through the rustle. The robins paused. Rabbits and badger froze. “The Whispering Hollow is not haunted. It is simply a hollow. The acorns you are worried about are perfectly safe, just a little further along, where they fell naturally.” He pointed at undisturbed grass. “As for Mrs Higgins’ petunia, I suspect a rather energetic field mouse looking for a midnight snack, not spectral breath. Your warnings have caused quite a stir. Next time, a moment of closer observation would be wise before spreading such alarming news.”

The robins looked at each other, chests deflating. The badger grumbled and retreated a little. The rabbits twitched toward the grass Fig had indicated. One particularly plump robin, who introduced himself as Flit, lowered his head. “It did sound very dramatic when the wind rustled the leaves so fiercely.”

A thoughtful quiet. Then Comet pointed toward the signpost, where the fireflies were dancing in a wild joyous ballet. “Look. They know it’s not scary.”

The tiny lights winked and swirled, denser than before, as if the pause at the post had been a rehearsal. The air filled with a soft contented hum. A rabbit ventured as far as the undisturbed grass Fig had indicated and found acorns exactly where a rat with a habit of facts had said they would be. Panic faded into the simple quiet beauty of a moonlit night. Creatures dispersed with a murmur of understanding. The hawthorn kept a few moths. The hollow kept its watchful silence, which now sounded less like a held breath and more like an ordinary wood sleeping.

Fig watched them go, satisfaction warm as a sunbeam. Comet chased a stray firefly, leaping and tumbling. They did not need to name the lesson. The hollow stayed a hollow. The fireflies stayed a show.

“You were brilliant,” Comet said, bouncing over. “Though a little bit of real adventure wouldn’t hurt.”

Fig chuckled, a rumble surprisingly deep for his size. His gaze swept the tranquil woods. “Perhaps. But the greatest ones are often the ones where we discover that what we feared was never truly there.”

They turned toward the warm glow of Leo’s lamp. The fireflies faded. The Whispering Hollow kept its uneventful slumber. Back through the window, the house still breathing sleep, Fig curled in his bedding. Comet’s copper tail settled last. The moon, higher now, laid its gentle light on gravestones, signpost, and two small adventurers who had spoken plainly and gone home.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
